blocks.md: Cargo builds with **profiles**: predefined sets of compiler settings. There are two main ones. `cargo build` uses the **`dev`** profile, tuned for fast compiles and good debugging; `cargo build --release` uses **`release`**, tuned for fast programs. You can override any setting in `Cargo.toml`:

blocks.code:
[profile.dev]
opt-level = 0     # the default: no optimization, fastest compile

[profile.release]
opt-level = 3     # the default: maximum optimization
# popular tweaks
lto = true        # link-time optimization across crates
codegen-units = 1 # slower to build, often a faster binary
panic = "abort"   # no unwinding (chapter 9)
debug = true      # keep debug info for profilers

[profile.dev.package."*"]
opt-level = 2     # optimize dependencies even in dev builds
blocks.explain: `opt-level` ranges from 0 to 3 (plus `"s"` and `"z"` to optimize for size). Debug builds also check integer overflow and panic on it; release builds wrap instead (chapter 3). The full list is in the Cargo book.

blocks.title: Documentation comments
blocks.md: Good documentation makes a crate usable. **Documentation comments** start with three slashes, `///`, support Markdown, and document the item that follows. `cargo doc` turns them into HTML, the same format as the standard library's docs; `cargo doc --open` builds docs for your crate and all its dependencies and opens them in a browser.

blocks.explain: `//!` documents the **enclosing** item, here the crate itself, and goes at the top of `src/lib.rs`. It is shown on the crate's front page. The example in `# Examples` is a doc test (chapter 11): `cargo test` runs it.

blocks.title: Sections crate authors commonly use
rows: how to call it; doubles as a test
the situations in which the function panics
for functions returning `Result`: which errors, and when
for `unsafe` functions: the invariants callers must uphold (chapter 20)

blocks.title: Intra-doc links
blocks.md: Write ``[`Vec`]`` or ``[`Config::build`]`` in a doc comment and rustdoc turns it into a link to that item's page, checked at build time. Hidden lines in examples start with `# `: they run but are not shown, which keeps examples focused.

blocks.title: A convenient public API with pub use

blocks.explain: Now users write `use art::{PrimaryColor, mix};`, and the docs front page lists the re-exports. The old paths still work. Libraries such as `serde` and `tokio` do this extensively.

blocks.title: Flatten an API with pub use
blocks.md: `main` wants to write `shapes::Circle` and `shapes::area`, but the items live deeper, in `shapes::kinds` and `shapes::math`. Add two `pub use` lines inside `mod shapes` so `main` compiles unchanged.

blocks.title: Publishing to crates.io
blocks.md: [crates.io](https://crates.io) is the community's package registry; `cargo` downloads dependencies from it. Publishing your own crate takes four steps:

steps.title: 1. Log in
steps.md: Create an account on crates.io (with a GitHub account), get an API token from your account settings, and store it locally. The token is a secret: never share it.
steps.code:
$ cargo login
please paste the token found on https://crates.io/me below

steps.title: 2. Add metadata
steps.md: A crate needs a unique `name`, a `description` and a `license` (an SPDX identifier). `cargo publish` tells you what is missing.
steps.code:
[package]
name = "guessing_game"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"
description = "A fun game where you guess what number the computer has chosen."
license = "MIT OR Apache-2.0"

steps.title: 3. Publish
steps.md: `cargo publish` packages and uploads the crate. **A publish is permanent**: the version can never be overwritten or deleted, so that every project depending on it keeps building.
steps.code:
$ cargo publish
    Updating crates.io index
   Packaging guessing_game v0.1.0 (file:///projects/guessing_game)
   Verifying guessing_game v0.1.0 (file:///projects/guessing_game)
   Uploaded guessing_game v0.1.0 to registry `crates-io`

steps.title: 4. New versions
steps.md: Change `version` following **Semantic Versioning**: patch (`0.1.1`) for fixes, minor (`0.2.0`) for compatible additions (for 0.x crates, minor bumps may break), major (`1.0.0` → `2.0.0`) for breaking changes. Then `cargo publish` again.

steps.title: 5. Yanking
steps.md: A broken version cannot be deleted, but it can be **yanked**: new projects will not pick it, while existing projects with it in their `Cargo.lock` keep working. `--undo` reverses it.

blocks.title: How Cargo picks versions
blocks.md: `rand = "0.8.5"` in `[dependencies]` means `^0.8.5`: any version compatible with 0.8.5, so at least 0.8.5 and below 0.9.0. `Cargo.lock` records the exact versions resolved, so builds are reproducible until you run `cargo update`. *Programming Rust* recommends committing `Cargo.lock` for applications; for libraries it is optional.

blocks.title: A convenient public API
blocks.goal: Re-export items with pub use so users can reach them from the crate root, and finish the mix function.
blocks.behavior:
The crate has `pub mod kinds` (the two color enums) and `pub mod utils` (`mix`). The tests use `crate::PrimaryColor`, `crate::SecondaryColor` and `crate::mix` from the **root**, so:
- Add `pub use` re-exports at the crate root for `PrimaryColor`, `SecondaryColor` and `mix`.
- Implement `mix`: Red+Yellow is Orange, Yellow+Blue is Green, Red+Blue is Purple, in either order. Mixing a color with itself returns `None`, so `mix` returns `Option<SecondaryColor>`.
- Add a documentation comment to `mix` with an `# Examples` heading (the tests cannot check this, but do it anyway).
hints: `pub use self::kinds::{PrimaryColor, SecondaryColor};` and `pub use self::utils::mix;` at the top of the file.
Match on the pair: `match (c1, c2) { (Red, Yellow) | (Yellow, Red) => Some(Orange), ... _ => None }` with `use PrimaryColor::*; use SecondaryColor::*;` inside the function.
blocks.solution_explain: The re-exports add new public paths without moving code, so `crate::utils::mix` still works. The doc example uses the crate's name with dashes turned into underscores (`ch14_api`), because a doc test is compiled as an external user of the crate.

questions.q: What is the difference between `///` and `//!`?
options: `///` documents the next item; `//!` documents the enclosing item, such as the crate
questions.explanation: Put `//!` at the top of lib.rs for crate docs.

questions.q: What does `pub use self::kinds::PrimaryColor;` at the crate root do?
questions.explanation: A re-export adds a public path.

questions.q: You published version 1.0.1 with a serious bug. What can you do?
questions.explanation: Publishes are permanent; yanking prevents new uses.
Caret requirements allow compatible (same major) updates.

points: Profiles (`dev`, `release`) set optimization and checks; override them in `[profile.*]`.
`///` documents items, `//!` the enclosing module or crate; `cargo doc --open` shows the HTML.
Common doc sections: Examples, Panics, Errors, Safety; examples are tested.
`pub use` re-exports give users a flat, convenient API without changing your layout.
`cargo publish` is permanent; use Semantic Versioning and `cargo yank` for bad versions.

terms.def: A named set of build settings in Cargo, such as dev and release.
How much the compiler optimizes, from 0 (none) to 3 (most).
Making an item available at another path with pub use.
The Rust community's public registry of crates.

Version numbers MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH where a major bump signals breaking changes.
